from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Putnam problems prioritize insight over computation.",
            "Shift your focus toward pattern recognition.",
            "Don't brute-force; look for elegant structures."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Putnam Mindset: Beyond Calculation", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.title.set_color(WHITE)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Using SVG asset
        icon = SVGMobject("/scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/calculator.svg", color="#FFD700")
        self.place_at_grid(icon, 'C5', scale_factor=1.2)
        self.play(FadeIn(icon))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFD700")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        highlight = SurroundingRectangle(self.title, color="#FF4500", buff=0.1)
        self.play(Create(highlight))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FF4500")
        self.wait(2)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite Toolkit: The Power of Invariants", [
            "Invariants remain constant despite dynamic change.",
            "Use invariants to track system state.",
            "Parity and coloring often reveal hidden answers."
        ])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        invariant_text = Text("Invariant", font_size=40, color="#00CED1")
        scale_icon = SVGMobject("/scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/scale.svg", color="#00CED1")
        scale_icon.next_to(invariant_text, UP)
        
        group1 = VGroup(invariant_text, scale_icon)
        self.place_in_area(group1, 'A3', 'B5', scale_factor=0.9)
        self.play(FadeIn(group1))
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#00CED1"))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Represent shifting objects
        obj1 = Circle(radius=0.4, color="#ADFF2F", fill_opacity=0.5)
        obj2 = Square(side_length=0.7, color="#ADFF2F", fill_opacity=0.5)
        obj3 = RegularPolygon(n=3, radius=0.4, color="#ADFF2F", fill_opacity=0.5)
        
        objs = VGroup(obj1, obj2, obj3).arrange(RIGHT)
        self.place_in_area(objs, 'D3', 'E5', scale_factor=0.8)
        
        shape_label = Text("System State", font_size=20, color="#ADFF2F")
        self.place_at_grid(shape_label, 'F4', scale_factor=0.7)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(objs), FadeIn(shape_label))
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#ADFF2F"))
        
        # Animation: shift positions while maintaining visual
        self.play(objs.animate.shift(UP * 0.5), run_time=1)
        self.wait(0.5)
        self.play(objs.animate.shift(DOWN * 0.5), run_time=1)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Flash the invariant property using gear asset
        gear_icon = SVGMobject("/scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/gear.svg", color="#FF6347")
        self.place_at_grid(gear_icon, 'C6', scale_factor=0.8)
        
        highlight = SurroundingRectangle(objs, color="#FF6347", buff=0.1)
        self.play(Create(highlight), FadeIn(gear_icon))
        self.play(Indicate(highlight, color="#FF6347"))
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FF6347"))
        self.play(FadeOut(highlight), FadeOut(gear_icon))
        self.wait(2)

            "Extreme points often force global constraints.", 
            "The extreme principle collapses search spaces."
        ])

outline.topic: Mastering the Putnam: Strategy and Intuition

sections.title: The Putnam Mindset: Beyond Calculation
sections.content: Transition from mechanical computation to 'Pattern Recognition'. Introduce the core philosophy: Putnam problems prioritize elegant, often non-obvious insights over brute-force algebra.
sections.example: A squirrel hiding nuts in a grid: Instead of calculating every spot, use the Pigeonhole Principle to prove at least one cache contains a specific density.

sections.title: Prerequisite Toolkit: The Power of Invariants
sections.content: Define 'Invariants'—properties that remain unchanged despite dynamic transformations. Use a visual graph showing a system evolving while a central 'knot' remains constant.
sections.example: A robot changing colors on a chessboard: If a move always flips adjacent squares, the parity of the colors remains invariant. We use this to solve complex tiling problems.

sections.title: Strategic Heuristics: Extreme Principle & Descent
sections.content: Introduce the 'Extreme Principle': If a set exists, consider the most extreme element (max/min). Visual: A mountain peak diagram where identifying the summit collapses the search space.
sections.example: Consider a set of points in the plane; look at the pair with the minimum distance. This 'local' extreme often forces a 'global' constraint that solves the problem instantly.

sections.title: Symmetry and Reduction
sections.content: Teach how to reduce complexity by identifying symmetries. Use visual overlays of rotational or reflective symmetry applied to complex geometric equations to simplify them.
sections.example: A spinning mechanical gear system: By assuming rotational symmetry, we can reduce a 10-variable system into a single representative variable equation.

sections.title: Putting it Together: The Final Proof Architecture
sections.content: Summarize the 'Look, Simplify, Solve' workflow. Emphasize that a clear logical narrative (the proof) is as important as the numerical result.
sections.example: Final walkthrough: A complex integral problem solved by recognizing a hidden symmetry (a secret mirror image in the function) that makes the area cancel out to zero.
